subject: Business Models
title: Toys R Us: Leveraged Into Oblivion
description: A 60-second lesson on Toys R Us: Leveraged Into Oblivion.

hook.text: Toys R Us didn't fail because nobody bought toys. It failed because private equity loaded it with $5 billion in debt.

buildup.text: In 2005, Bain Capital and KKR bought Toys R Us in a leveraged buyout. The company borrowed to fund its own sale.

discovery.text: Debt payments of $400M/year drained cash that should have funded stores, online, and inventory improvements.

twist.text: While Toys R Us paid interest, Amazon invested in logistics. The debt-free competitor won with superior execution.

climax.text: Leveraged buyouts starve companies of investment capital. Toys R Us: a textbook case of debt killing operations.

punchline.text: $5B in debt, $400M/year in interest. Financial engineering killed the toy store.

quiz.question: What was the primary cause of Toys R Us's bankruptcy?
options: Massive debt from a leveraged buyout draining investment cash

details.summary: Toys R Us was the dominant toy retailer until a leveraged buyout in 2005 loaded it with 5.3 billion dollars in debt. Annual interest payments of 400 million drained capital needed for store improvements and e-commerce investment, leaving it unable to compete with Amazon and Walmart.
details.whyItMatters: Toys R Us shows how financial engineering can destroy an operationally viable business. The company was still generating positive operating income when it filed for bankruptcy; debt service simply consumed all available cash for investment and.
takeaways: Leveraged buyout loaded Toys R Us with 5.3 billion dollars in debt
400 million annual interest payments drained investment capital for years
The company filed for bankruptcy despite positive underlying operating income

faq.question: How did the leveraged buyout lead to Toys R Us's bankruptcy?
faq.answer: KKR, Bain Capital, and Vornado bought Toys R Us for 6.6 billion, financing mostly with debt placed on the company's balance sheet. Annual interest payments of 400 million consumed cash that should have funded store modernization, e-commerce, and competitive pricing.

faq.question: Was Toys R Us doomed even without the leveraged buyout?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. The company was profitable before the debt burden. With investment capital, it could have built a competitive online presence, improved store experiences, and maintained pricing parity. The LBO removed the financial flexibility needed to adapt to retail changes.
